Solving common problems¶

This chapter is arranged by symptom. Each entry names the likely cause and the fix that users have reported.

Almost everything here comes from user forums, not from the developer. Each fix says how well it is supported: “confirmed by several users” means more than one person reported that the fix worked, and “single report” means one user posted it and nobody confirmed it. Most reports date from Priroda 6 to 10 (about 2009–2015); a few are from 2008 or from 2016–2026. Where a problem may have been fixed in later builds, the entry says so.

Note

Most fixes below have not been checked against a current Priroda binary. Where a test run on version 25 (2025.02.28) confirmed or contradicted a report, the entry says so.

The input is not read, or is read wrongly¶

When Priroda cannot parse the input it often stops early, with little or no explanation. Just as often a mistake is silently ignored and the run goes on: in version 25 a group written as &dft was skipped, an unknown theory ran Hartree–Fock, an unknown task only set up the job, keywords in a group the task does not read were not checked, and atomic numbers written as 8.0 gave a wrong molecule (see below). Before anything else, open the output and check what it echoed back: the Memory: and Disk: lines, the formula: line, the summary box (number of atoms, charge, multiplicity, method, functional), the scf: line and the grid: line. If a value you set is not shown there, Priroda did not read it.

Output stops after molecule input: ''¶

The line molecule input: '' itself is printed in every run. It is a problem only when the output ends there or continues with garbled text.

Cause. In almost every reported case the input file had Windows (CRLF) line endings. The tail of the output then shows a mangled keyword followed by ?, for example ' ?matrix, ?rtesian or 'z-matrix' ?. Inputs saved as Unicode, or edited in Word, were also reported not to be read. Word’s “save as text” still writes CRLF line endings.

Fix. Save the input as plain ASCII text with Unix (LF) line endings, for example with dos2unix input.in. Notepad++ and Far Manager (Shift+F2 in the editor) can also convert line endings. Use straight quotes only. Several users confirmed this fix. Running dos2unix on a file that already has LF endings does no harm.

The molecule is wrong: odd formula, extra atoms¶

Atomic numbers written as real numbers (8.0 instead of 8) in $molecule. The atom lines are read as a stream of numbers, so everything after the first .0 shifts. In version 25 there is no error: water written with 8.0 and 1.0 ran as four atoms, an oxygen and three empty centres with Z=0, with the formula __3O and a meaningless energy. An older version was reported to stop with illegal charge/multiplicity instead. Write atomic numbers as integers, and check the formula: line and the atom count at the top of every output.

One experienced user also advises avoiding Cyrillic letters and spaces in the computer name, directory names and file names. In the case where he gave this advice, fixing the line endings alone was reported to solve the problem.

task=scan runs an optimization, or nothing works on one machine¶

An input that runs on one computer but not on another, or a task=scan that silently runs a plain optimization, has been traced to the same encoding problem: an input edited in Word or saved as Unicode. Fix it as above.

Two task= lines in one input do not chain jobs, and no error is printed. In version 25 only the last one ran (task=optimize then task=hessian gave just a Hessian); in a 2011 report (version 6) only the first one ran. The only combined task name is task=optimize+hessian; see task. A user in 2011 added that even this one did not work in all versions. Run other sequences, such as optimization followed by NMR, as separate jobs.

The basis file is not found¶

  • Quote file names with straight double quotes: basis="3z.bas". Two single quotes (basis=''3z.bas'') give error opening file ''3z.bas'', and typographic quotes copied from a web page or word processor fail too.

  • Give an absolute path to the basis file if Priroda is not started from the directory that contains it. One user’s parallel run aborted with MPI_Abort until he wrote the full basis path in the input. In version 25 a relative name worked with the file in the current directory, in a serial and in a 2-process run.

  • The relativistic basis file basis4.in needs four=1 in $control. Without it the job stops right after the Basis set input: line, with 1? as the only message (version 25). The user who first reported this confirmed the fix.

  • The name given in set must exist in the basis file.

The input or output file cannot be opened¶

On Linux the usual cause is a wrong path. Check it with ls -l before blaming Priroda. In one reported case the directory in the command line simply did not exist. Work in a directory you own and can write to (for example ~/priroda), cd into it, and run the binary with an explicit path, since the current directory is normally not in PATH:

cd ~/priroda
./p job.in job.out

File names are case-sensitive, unlike keywords. One user of an older version saw the extra complaint 0: output file 'tasK.out'? when the file name contained capital letters. Version 25 wrote an output file with capital letters in its name without complaint.

On Windows, cd into the folder with the input before running p.exe input.in output.out. One user still got cannot open input file after doing that, and the thread never found the cause.

Output stops at 0: opening file /tmp/... (Windows)¶

Old Windows builds put scratch files in /tmp when nothing else is set (the output echoes Disk:   1 GB '/tmp'), and Windows has no /tmp. The Linux version 25 has the same default and also honours TMPDIR. Set the scratch directory explicitly, for example $system path=. $end, or set the TMPDIR environment variable before starting the program. This is the oldest known problem in both forums and the fix is well established. See path.

$scf settings are ignored or rejected¶

The parser has a problem when convergence is directly followed by another keyword in $scf. In version 25,

$scf convergence=1e-7 iterations=250 $end

stops the run after the basis-set echo with *** error in '$scf' : unknown name terations. The message names iterations with its first letters missing. How many are missing depended on the machine, not on the value: the same input printed unknown name erations with the p4_d executable on another computer, for every value tried, as forum users of 2015 builds also reported. With procedure=bfgs between them, $scf convergence=1e-7 procedure=bfgs iterations=250 $end, both values are read; one forum user found that the pair worked only with procedure=bfgs.

Further tests on version 25 narrowed it down. The problem is a convergence= with one value followed by iterations=, also on the next line; other keywords after it, such as restrict= or procedure=, were read correctly. Both of these work:

$scf convergence=1e-7,1e-3 iterations=250 $end
$scf iterations=250 convergence=1e-7 $end

So give iterations before convergence, or give convergence two values, and confirm the values in the scf: echo line of the output, for example scf: conv = 1.0e-07, 1.0e-03; iter=250,16.

SCF does not converge or diverges¶

Recognizing the problem¶

Users report that Priroda’s SCF usually converges well, better than in many other programs. Trouble mostly comes with metals in low oxidation states, where the electronic structure has some multiconfigurational character, with very large basis sets, and with diffuse functions.

Signs of trouble in the SCF table:

  • hmin values that keep growing in magnitude, or a line such as h = -25.15!;

  • lowest eigenvalue = ...!!! lines with large negative numbers;

  • an energy that rises from one macro-iteration to the next;

  • no convergence!, in older versions followed by SCF is far from convergence.

Warning

In version 25, a single-point run whose SCF hits the iteration limit prints no convergence! and then carries on: it prints an energy, orbitals and properties and exits normally. An OH radical with default settings did this after the default 32 iterations, still creeping towards convergence; with iterations=100 it converged after 34. Always check for converged!.

The DFT SCF runs on a coarse grid first and then switches to the final grid; the switch is marked by a new grid: line with the number of points. A short jump in the gradient at that point is normal. Steady growth after it is not (see Divergence after the switch to the fine grid (open-shell transition-metal complex)).

Check the input first¶

In one well-documented failure, several input errors were present besides the SCF trouble. Before changing SCF settings, check:

  • Multiplicity. mult must match the electron count. One failing input gave mult=0 for an odd number of electrons, and the summary box showed Spin multiplicity 0.

  • Theory and functional. A hybrid functional with theory=dft is wrong; see Hybrid functional silently ignored.

  • Basis. Non-native basis sets and diffuse functions converge badly. A non-native basis file must also supply a fitting (auxiliary) basis, and a badly prepared one causes trouble. Use a native basis, or start from a geometry optimized in one.

  • Geometry. A very poor starting geometry can by itself prevent SCF convergence. Pre-optimize with a cheap pure functional (for example PBE with theory=dft) before switching to the target method.

Restart from saved vectors¶

This technique is recommended on both forums (by amg and by amge, who may be the same person), and the limor1 pri driver script automates it:

  1. Cap the number of SCF iterations at a moderate value, for example iterations=10 in $scf. Choose the cap so that hmin does not run away.

  2. Have Priroda write its vectors with save in $control.

  3. When the SCF ends with no convergence! (older versions stopped with SCF is far from convergence), add $guess read=1 $end (see read) and rerun with the latest geometry.

  4. Repeat until the SCF converges.

$control
 task=optimize
 theory=dft
 basis="basis.in"
 save=job.vec
$end
$scf iterations=10 $end
$guess read=1 $end

An optimization in version 25 does not stop when the SCF of one step fails to converge: it goes on to the next step, which starts from the last orbitals. In a test on water with iterations=3, the first step ended with no convergence!, the later steps converged, and the optimization reached the same energy as a normal run in the same number of steps. So the loop above matters mostly for single points and for the first SCF of a hard case; check every step of an optimization for no convergence! all the same.

In version 25 the output of a restarted run shows Initial Guess (-1) and vectors from 'job.vec'; a normal start shows Initial Guess (2). Each restart continues from where the previous run stopped, and goes straight to the final grid instead of starting again on the coarse one. In a test on a 22-atom copper complex with 3 iterations per run, the loop converged in the fourth run, after about 12 iterations in all.

Leave out the $guess line in the first run. Vectors from a converged run of an easier case, or of the same molecule at another geometry, also work as a starting point.

Switch the SCF procedure and tighten the grid¶

The default procedure is Newton–Raphson (nr). If it blows up, try bfgs, and the other way round. One experienced user recommends this setting for difficult cases, “which is nearly all of them”:

$scf
 convergence=1e-7
 procedure=bfgs
 iterations=250
$end
$grid
 accuracy=1e-9
$end

He notes that the default 16 iterations of the versions of that time are too few for many jobs; version 25 defaults to 32. If you tighten convergence to 1e-8, make the grid finer as well, 1e-9 or 1e-10 (see accuracy).

Note

The user who asked never reported whether this fixed the failing job. bfgs is not a cure-all: in the case in the next section it may have been part of the problem.

Divergence after the switch to the fine grid (open-shell transition-metal complex)¶

Symptom. A doublet Cu(II) complex (OLYP/L2, restrict=0, procedure=BFGS, $grid acc=1e-12, task=hessian) converged on the coarse grid. After the switch to the final grid it oscillated for about 30 iterations and then diverged, with the total energy reaching +29 hartree. BLYP behaved the same way.

Note

The same molecule and SCF settings, run as a single point, converge in version 25: with the original BFGS settings in 48 iterations, and with the default Newton–Raphson procedure in 10 iterations and about half the time. The divergence did not reproduce. If you meet it in a current version, the fixes below are still the ones to try.

Fixes. Two experienced users solved it in two ways, which they considered equivalent:

  • Run task=optimize+hessian instead of a single-point Hessian, and drop procedure=BFGS and iterations:

    $control task=optimize+hessian $end
$scf restrict=0 convergence=1e-10 $end

    Each optimization step then starts from the previous wavefunction. In version 25 this route converged the optimization of the complex in 6 steps, with every SCF converging, and the Hessian finished: 32 minutes in all on 8 processes, with one small imaginary frequency (6.11i cm⁻¹).

  • Save the wavefunction at the start of the optimization with save and read it into the Hessian job with $guess read=1. For an already optimized structure, the guess built from scratch turned out to be poor.

Open-shell singlets and broken symmetry¶

For an open-shell (broken-symmetry) singlet, start the unrestricted singlet from the vectors of the triplet. This is the route that worked in version 25 tests: run the triplet with save, then the singlet with restrict=0 and $guess read=1 (the program accepts vectors of another multiplicity). For O2 this converged, after many iterations, to a broken-symmetry singlet 0.048 hartree below the closed-shell one and 0.015 hartree above the triplet. Give such runs plenty of iterations, and check the result as described below.

This route works only when the triplet’s orbitals themselves give the singlet an asymmetric start. For O2 they did, because the two singly occupied π* orbitals are degenerate. For stretched H2 they did not: started from the triplet’s vectors, the singlet fell back to the restricted solution.

Neither the atomic spin populations (print=+charges) nor the orbital energies showed that this solution was broken-symmetry: in O2 both came out the same for broken-symmetry and closed-shell solutions, because the two π* orbitals are spread equally over both atoms. What showed it was the energy of a second run from the same triplet vectors with restrict=1, which fell back to the closed-shell energy. Use the same check when the spins do not decide.

The older sources recommend instead an unrestricted calculation with the HOMO and LUMO of the guess mixed:

$scf restrict=0 $end
$guess mix=1 $end

Warning

In version 25 tests mix=1 had no visible effect: no run with it broke the symmetry, not even stretched H2 with UHF, the textbook case. Use the triplet-vectors route above, and check the result.

See restrict and mix. In version 25 tests, restrict=0 mix=1 converged back to the restricted solution for singlet O2 with theory=dft (PBE) and for the Cr2 dimer with both the default and the bfgs procedure: the energies equalled the closed-shell ones exactly. With theory=ridft (PBE1) the O2 run also gave identical alpha and beta orbital energies, but no closed-shell reference was run, so that case is undecided. The same happened for H2 stretched to 2.5 Å, with both HF and PBE, for every integer value of mix tried (1, 2, −1, 10, 45, 90): the singlet stayed at the restricted energy, −0.8632 hartree for HF, although the triplet lies at −0.9972. An unrestricted SCF in Priroda keeps whatever symmetry its starting orbitals have, and mix=1 did not supply the asymmetry.

In a 2011 forum report with non-RI pure DFT (theory=dft, PBE or BLYP), restrict=0 mix=1 likewise converged back to the restricted solution, with identical energies and identical alpha and beta orbital energies. With RI-DFT the same user got an unrestricted energy about 3 microhartree lower, which he took as broken symmetry. Another user notes that pure GGA functionals often do not break symmetry, and suggests a hybrid (with theory=ridft) or a Hartree–Fock calculation first.

LUMO below the HOMO¶

In the orbital energies printed after the SCF, the lowest virtual orbital normally lies above the highest occupied one. If it lies below, either the SCF has settled in an excited configuration, or the molecule has a partly filled set of degenerate orbitals that a closed-shell calculation cannot fill in order.

The second case happened for singlet O2 in version 25 tests. In a closed-shell (mult=1) run the pair occupies one of the two degenerate π* orbitals. The occupied orbital ended at −0.178 hartree, above the empty one at −0.219. Starting with the two orbitals swapped (na, nb; whether the swap took effect is not shown in the output), or from the triplet’s vectors with restrict=1, gave the same state and energy, since filling the other π* orbital is equivalent by symmetry. For such molecules the closed-shell energy is not a meaningful singlet energy: use an unrestricted broken-symmetry run (see Open-shell singlets and broken symmetry) or the high-spin state.

The first case could not be produced in version 25 tests. Water started with its HOMO and LUMO swapped, either from the default guess or from vectors read from a file, went back to the ground state every time; the swap only made the SCF take two to three times more iterations. In the version 25 tests, the only persistent case was the degenerate shell of O2.

Note

If an excited configuration does turn up in a molecule without degenerate orbitals, two tools are available: start from other vectors ($guess read=1 with vectors of a related calculation), or reorder the starting orbitals with na and nb. Neither was tested for this manual on such a case, because none was found.

Heavy elements¶

For scalar-relativistic pure DFT with the heaviest atoms, the v5 documentation suggests d1small=1; without it, the quadratically convergent SCF may fail.

If an orbital ordering problem is suspected, na and nb reorder the starting vectors.

Cases without a known fix¶

  • An HF reference for CCSD diverged for a small closed-shell molecule (7 atoms, set=L1, restrict=0). The change column stuck at 0.50000000. Nobody replied. Running a closed-shell molecule with restrict=0 was unusual and may be worth changing.

  • An HfCl2 molecule (PBE, four=1, basis4.in, set=L3, accuracy=1e-10) would not converge. Nobody replied. Two things in the posted input are worth checking in such a case (this is the manual’s observation, not a tested fix): it had $guess read=1 in the same job that wrote the vectors with save=, so the start depended on whatever vector file already existed; and it used mult=1 for a d² Hf(II) compound.

Geometry optimization problems¶

The optimization does not converge within steps¶

The default limit is 128 steps in version 25 and 50 in older versions (see steps). When the limit is reached, the output just ends: there is no message and no MOL> block. Dft.rtf, an older unofficial Russian description, warns that an optimization not converged after about 50 steps very likely has something wrong with it, and that computing a Hessian first helps in many cases. So don’t simply raise steps. What users do:

  • Restart from the last geometry. The limor1 pri script restarts Priroda from the last geometry whenever an optimization runs out of steps. This helps when the optimizer cycles around one geometry even after 300 steps.

  • Supply a Hessian. Run task=hessian, append its $Energy block (the eng> lines) to the input, and optimize again. See $Energy.

  • Use Cartesian coordinates. cartesian=1 is called a last resort on the v5 keyword page, but the limor1 conformers script uses it for automated runs, and one experienced user says floppy systems such as explicit solvation shells have to be optimized in Cartesian coordinates. In version 25 tests on CO2 and acetylene it needed 6 steps, against 12 and 24 in internal coordinates.

One experienced user found Priroda’s optimizer weaker than Gaussian’s, while its SCF is stronger (2013).

Crash with process 0 got signal 6 and too few¶

Symptom. The optimization dies with process 0 got signal 6. In the output of the last step, the INTERNAL COORDINATES table ends with too few.

Fix. Optimize in Cartesian coordinates:

$optimize cartesian=1 $end

This was the answer from one experienced user; the asker did not report back.

The crash could not be reproduced in version 25 tests with molecules that become linear, the usual suspects for running short of internal coordinates. CO2 and acetylene started bent converged in internal coordinates: the optimizer rebuilt its coordinate set when the molecule became linear (from 5 to 4 coordinates for CO2, from 9 to 7 for acetylene) and carried on. They needed 12 and 24 steps, against 6 each with cartesian=1.

The optimization “converges” in one step¶

A run that reports convergence after a single step, with an energy that is not a number, did not optimize anything: the SCF failed on the first step. See NaN energy, or an optimization that stops after one step.

A symmetric structure stays symmetric¶

Without the symmetry options, Priroda works in C1, but a symmetric starting geometry often stays symmetric through an optimization that converges normally, and the Hessian then shows a saddle point. If the optimization did not break the symmetry, always compute the Hessian. If it has an imaginary frequency, paste its $Energy block into the input, displace the geometry along that mode if needed, and optimize again.

Version 25 can also use symmetry on purpose: $molecule sym=1,0.01 detects the point group and symmetrizes the input geometry, and $optimize sym=1 keeps that symmetry during the optimization. Both options are needed. See $molecule sym and $optimize symmetry.

A scan starts from a mangled geometry¶

Cause. Priroda’s dihedral angles have the opposite sign to the convention used by Molden, MOPAC and GAMESS. A dihedral value copied from another program makes the first scan point a scrambled structure that has nothing to do with the input geometry.

Fix. Flip the sign of every dihedral value taken from another program. The user who hit this confirmed that flipping the signs fixed it. The user who answered (amge) had reported the sign difference on qchem.ru in 2008, for “all versions” of that time. Version 25 still uses the opposite sign: a Z-matrix dihedral of +100° gave Cartesian coordinates with a standard (IUPAC) dihedral of −100°, and a scan whose first value was −100° instead of +100° started by turning the molecule into its mirror image.

A scan that requested 10 points but computed only 7 (and 11 of 20) was reported once and never explained.

IRC gives only two points, or no curve¶

An IRC must start from a properly optimized transition state with an accurate Hessian in the input. Find the TS first (task=optimize with saddle=1), compute the Hessian there, check that it has exactly one imaginary frequency and that this mode is the reaction you want, and only then run task=irc. In one reported case, an IRC started from an unoptimized geometry gave two points with back=0 and no curve with back=1; an experienced user called this typical of an under-optimized geometry.

IRC stops with Vicinity of a Stationary Point(?) --- STOP.¶

This message is also the normal end of an IRC that has reached a minimum: a version 25 test IRC of the ammonia inversion ended with it after 7 points, at the minimum. It is a problem only when it comes early.

On the first IRC step this means that the energy did not go down on that step. The reported fix is to change the step size; see radius:

  • on a very flat barrier top, increase the step so that it reaches the slope;

  • on a very narrow barrier, such as a proton transfer, decrease it, because a step suited to heavy atoms throws the proton too far.

This advice comes from one experienced user.

In a version 25 test on a hydrogen shift (HCN ⇄ HNC), step sizes of 0.03 and 0.1 (the default) reached both minima without stopping early; 0.3, run toward HCN only, also reached its minimum. So the default is a sensible start even for a light atom. The step size changed the cost and how close to the minimum the path ended: 60–69 points with 0.03, 19–21 with 0.1, and 7 with 0.3, which stopped farthest from the minimum (gradient 0.010 against 0.0003–0.006).

An IRC can also end with Energy Minimum Passed --- STOP. right after the Vicinity message, when its last point overshot the minimum and came out higher in energy than the one before. This is a normal end too.

IRC ends near a minimum but not in it¶

This is normal: always re-optimize both IRC endpoints. An IRC can also stop on a flat shelf where the gradient is small, or at another TS. Then compute a Hessian at the stopping point and run a new IRC from there; this sometimes has to be repeated three or four times. Priroda has no option to recompute the Hessian every n steps.

Wrong or suspicious results¶

Hybrid functional silently ignored¶

Cause. Hybrid functionals (B3LYP, PBE0/PBE1, …) are applied only with theory=ridft. With theory=dft or theory=tddft, older versions (reported for v6 to v8) ran without any error message but used zero exact exchange: the exact-exchange part was simply dropped, so the result matched neither the hybrid nor a pure GGA. The developer was told about it and, according to a user who corresponded with him, did not intend to change it.

Newer builds (reported in 2014) refuse with theory=dft: the job prints Basis set input: twice and stops with application called MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1) - process 0 (on stderr), before the summary box. Another user reproduced it with a known-good input, and version 25 does the same.

Warning

With theory=tddft the trap is still open in version 25. A water run with functional=PBE1 showed PBE1 in the summary box, finished normally and printed excited states, but the exchange energy was −6.61 instead of about −8.95 hartree and the total energy was about 2.2 hartree too high: the exact-exchange part was simply left out. Any TDDFT result with a hybrid functional is wrong.

Fix. Use theory=ridft for every hybrid ground-state calculation, and a pure GGA functional (PBE, the default) for TDDFT. There is no hybrid TDDFT in Priroda.

NaN energy, or an optimization that stops after one step¶

Cause. The SCF energy on the first step is not a number, so the optimizer stops at once and reports convergence. The reported causes are all basis problems:

  • No basis for an element. A molecule containing Bi was run with 3z.bas, which covers only Z ≤ 54. Use sbk.bas (ECP basis up to Rn, Z ≤ 86) or basis4.in with four=1.

  • ECP not read. In one case nothing was computed and there was no error message. The output showed zeros for one element in the basis table, and no sign that the ECP had been read. The cause was a defect in the user’s basis file; 20+sbk.bas worked.

  • A NaN at the first SCF iteration for [PtCl6]2- with the St-rsc-97 ECP basis went away after switching to the sbk(u) basis. Why that basis failed is not known.

What to check. In the output, the ECP should be read before the basis, and every atom in the basis table should have a non-zero number of basis functions.

TDDFT oscillator strengths are all zero¶

A closed-shell TDDFT run on version 25 printed non-zero oscillator strengths in its Electronic Spectrum: table with the default settings.

The reported cause of all-zero values: with restrict=0 set explicitly, singlet and triplet excitations get mixed. Use $scf restrict=1 (the default for a closed-shell singlet) and compute one multiplicity per run. The user who reported the problem confirmed the fix.

The dipole moment is zero¶

Version 6 printed dipole =   0.000000 au (  0.000000 D) for every molecule when relativistic basis sets were used, even with task=dipole. Version 8 and later print a value.

Energies differ between Priroda versions¶

Newer builds are faster but give slightly different total energies for the same input. Do not compare close energies computed with different versions; within one version the comparison is fine.

The printed energy components do not add up to E¶

The line T = ... V = ... J = ... Ex = ... Ec = ... does not include the nuclear repulsion energy, so the components do not sum to E. This is not an error: E = T + V + J + Ex + Ec + E(nn). The answer came from the developer, relayed by a user.

Thermochemistry of single atoms¶

For a monoatomic species the enthalpy has an extra RT, and the rotational entropy is printed as -inf. Correct these by hand and keep only the translational terms.

Results depend on the number of processes¶

In one unstable TS search started from a poor guess, the optimization followed different paths with different -np. Normally the results differ only in insignificant digits.

Memory, disk and scratch errors¶

All $system limits apply per MPI process. With disk=10 on four processes, up to 40 GB can be used.

need … bytes.¶

Cause. The memory limit in $system is too small for the job. Version 25 stops right after the basis-set echo with a line such as need 12544 + 7905408 = 7917952 bytes. (here for water with mem=2); the last number, in bytes (here about 7.6 MB), is what the job needs at that point. Set memory (in MB) above it.

malloc(...) failed¶

Cause. Priroda could not allocate the memory requested in memory, plus any RAM disk requested with a negative disk. The number in the message is the request in bytes.

Fix. Ask for less than the node really has free:

  • With a RAM disk, memory plus |disk| (both in MB), times the number of processes, must fit in physical RAM. One experienced user’s example for a 24 GB node, memory=9000 disk=-14000, assumes one process per node. Another user’s limit, memory=9250 disk=-9250, fits this rule.

  • The 32-bit Windows (Cygwin) builds cannot allocate more than about 1 GB. 512 MB was enough for most DFT jobs. Several users confirmed this limit. The 64-bit Windows build with cygwin1.dll is reported to have no such limit.

A message beginning We need 1.5 GB of memory... was reported once. One reply guessed that it is about RAM (memory=), not disk space. It may be an older form of the need … bytes. message above.

out of disk space¶

Symptom. 0: out of disk space (VNNNN), <N>KB, or a similar message naming another array, such as (ci.Rnvvo). Version 25 with a 1 MB RAM disk (disk=-1) printed 0: out of disk space (grid_W), 8213824.

Fix.

  • Raise disk above the amount reported. Remember that the value is per process.

  • Conventional MP2 is very disk-hungry. Use theory=rimp2 instead.

  • Check that cartesian or z-matrix in $molecule matches the coordinates you actually gave; wrong coordinates can make the job far bigger than intended.

Each scratch file is created for 1 GB per process and filled as needed. Jobs needing more than 20–45 GB of scratch were, in one experienced user’s words, not worth their cost.

A failure to read a scratch file during MP2 (0: read file ./tmp/...) was given the same fix.

A small RI-MP2 job does not fit in memory¶

A 7-atom RI-MP2 job with four=1, basis4.in and set=L22 claimed not to fit in memory however much was given, while smaller and larger basis sets ran. A second user reproduced it and got 0: write VMNN(11753704:14042536)?. The first user found that direct integrals avoid the problem:

$integral direct=1 $end

See direct.

Where scratch files go¶

Priroda writes scratch files to the directory given by path; if path is not set, to $TMPDIR; otherwise, in version 25, to /tmp (a 2020 user report said the directory of the input file). On a cluster, /tmp is often too small or quota-limited for large scratch files. Use the cluster’s local scratch area, or a RAM disk with a negative disk value. Never put scratch on NFS.

A job that stops while writing a scratch file, with a message like 0: write file /tmp/tmp9633.11 (leAX): fd=21 ..., was reported once (2020) during an analytic Hessian on a cluster. An experienced user replied that no path= was set, so scratch went to /tmp, probably on the master node, where quotas can make the job fail, and advised the cluster’s scratch area. The asker then tried a tmp folder and got the same error; the case was not resolved. Check the free space, the quotas and the disk= setting.

If Priroda does not get enough memory or scratch, it stops with an error; it does not fall back to a slower algorithm.

Slow runs: disk speed¶

Priroda is very demanding of disk speed. For all methods except GGA DFT, input.txt warns that performance degrades “terribly” if more than one process reads and writes large files on the same physical drive. Options, in order of preference:

  • keep scratch in RAM with a negative disk value (one cluster reported a 6× speed-up for RI-MP2);

  • give each process its own physical drive with a colon-separated path list;

  • if the job is disk-bound, switch to direct integrals with direct=1. This costs CPU time but can be much faster overall: one RI-MP2 optimization went from 2 to 20 steps per night.

Parallel and MPI problems¶

A parallel RI job hangs with no message¶

Cause. RI methods, RI-MP2 and RI-DFT included, hang forever if any process gets no work. This happens when the job is too small for the number of processes. Two experienced users confirmed it and called it a bug.

How to recognize it. After integral estimates, the output lists the blocks per node. In a normal run every node has work, as here; a hung job shows 0 blocks on some node:

    2892490 blocks,    103625770 integrals on node  0
    3681560 blocks,     91256706 integrals on node  1

Fix. Run small RI jobs on fewer processes, or on one core.

Older reports describe similar hangs: small jobs on many processors hang (v6/v7); MP2 on a 102-atom complex died with signal 8 on more than about 24 cores (v7, MVAPICH); a v6 Hessian on 4 cores could hang at Solving for responses .... The v6 advice was at most 2 cores for a Hessian and at most 4 for an optimization. Another user ran DFT, including Hessians, on 24–32 cores without trouble, so this advice is disputed. In 2018 an experienced user said the Windows builds run in parallel only from version 16, and that the v6 Hessian uses at most 2 cores, the v17 one 4 or more.

Little or no speed-up from more cores¶

  • Reports on DFT scaling within one node disagree: one experienced user found at most 10% more from 32 cores than from 6–8, while another measured 101, 63 and 37 s for the same optimization on 8, 12 and 24 cores.

  • For DFT, running across several nodes gives no gain; one experienced user said so on three occasions. RI-MP2 is different: in a v8 benchmark on 4 nodes with scratch in RAM it ran 6× faster than on 2 cores of one node.

  • In a DFT run most of the memory and all the disk I/O stay on rank 0, so spreading a DFT job over nodes does not spread its memory. RI-MP2 distributes memory better.

  • For throughput, several single-core jobs at once can beat one multi-core job when the jobs are not disk-bound.

  • For RI-MP2, the v5 documentation suggests a number of processes that divides the number of occupied orbitals.

Environment is too large (max is 193)¶

Symptom. A parallel run started with the mpiexec from the official site prints this line (once per process) and stops at once; no output file is written. Typically this happens inside a batch job.

Cause. That mpiexec refuses to start when the environment holds 193 or more variables. Batch systems add many variables of their own; a Slurm job in a version 25 test had 210.

Fix. Start it with a minimal environment:

env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$HOME" TMPDIR="$TMPDIR" ./mpiexec -np 4 ./p input.in output.out

See Batch systems for a complete job script.

Starting a parallel run on Linux¶

A parallel version 25 run must be started through an MPI launcher, such as the mpiexec from the official site: ./mpiexec -np 4 ./p job.in job.out. ./p -np 4 job.in job.out, which worked in versions 6 and 10, now stops with input file '-np'?.. With version 10, starting through the bundled mpiexec once failed with Error in system call mpiexec: No such file or directory or mpiexec could not exec p. Use absolute paths for the binary, the input, the output and the basis file.

The message OOPS: semop lock failed (with process N received signal 2 or 6) has two reported contexts:

  • as a secondary message after another fatal error, such as running out of disk. Fix the first error;

  • in v6 shared-memory runs on 7 cores. Fewer cores avoided it; cleaning semaphores with ipcrm did not help.

It also appeared for one user who ran as a normal user while the same input worked as root. That case was never resolved.

A run that stops producing output right after the header, while the process keeps using CPU, has been reported and called common. The only advice was to look for stray files named after the input or output in the input, output, program and home directories, and then to rule out causes one by one.

Windows¶

Old Windows builds were serial only. For a parallel 64-bit run (version 16 or later), users report this setup:

  1. From a 64-bit Cygwin installation with OpenMPI, copy cygwin1.dll, cyggcc_s-seh-1.dll, cygmpi-12.dll, cygopen-pal-13.dll, cygopen-rte-12.dll and orterun.exe next to the Priroda executable. Take cygwin1.dll from the same Cygwin installation, because the other DLLs work only with it. These are the names from a 2017 Cygwin. A 2018 report says newer OpenMPI packages ship cygopen-pal-40.dll and cygopen-rte-40.dll instead; take those.

  2. To run outside the Cygwin terminal, create a dev directory one level above the directory you start Priroda from, with subdirectories shm and mqueue. For Priroda in C:\Priroda 16 that means C:\dev\shm and C:\dev\mqueue. Without them Cygwin prints Warning: '/dev/shm' does not exists or is not a directory.

  3. Set TMPDIR and start the run from cmd.exe:

    cd /d "C:\Priroda 16"
set TMPDIR="%TEMP%"
"orterun.exe" -np 2 ./p16_64_parallel.exe "C:\Work\file.in" "C:\Work\file.out"

    This is the command as posted. In cmd.exe, set TMPDIR="%TEMP%" keeps the quotes as part of the value; set "TMPDIR=%TEMP%" does not. Which form the Cygwin build expects was not tested.

  4. If the program is in a system directory such as C:\Program Files, run it as administrator.

Network problems reported with this setup:

  • On a PC connected by WiFi that also has a LAN adapter, OpenMPI failed with tcp_peer_send_blocking: send() to socket 12 failed. Disabling the LAN adapter fixed it (single report).

  • With the Ethernet cable unplugged, only some cores were used. Plugging it back in fixed it (single report).

A 2021 attempt to follow this recipe on Windows 10 failed with an error that was posted only as a screenshot; no fix was posted. One user runs Priroda under WSL on Windows instead; no details of that setup were posted.

Warning

Not every build on the official site is reliable. A note there once said that the w64/*.exe 64-bit Cygwin builds had a DFT/ECP bug. If a Windows build misbehaves, ask the developer which build you should be running.
